column1: The National Board

column2: (1) The meetings of the National Board shall be held at the call of the chairman, or in his absence at the call of the executive committee, at least once in each month unless otherwise directed by the National Board.

column1: (3) The decision of the majority of the National Board at any meeting shall be the decision of the National Board and in the event of a tie the chairman shall have a casting vote.

column2: The chief executive officer of the National Board shall carry out the directions of and shall perform such duties as are assigned to him by the executive committee.

column2: A regional board may make such rules as may seem expedient for the conduct of its business and proceedings not inconsistent with the provisions of the order or of these by-laws.

column1: (2) A regional board shall comply with any request of and shall give effect to any order or direction by the National Board.

column1: National War Labour Board
To Chairmen and Chief Executive Officers Regional War Labour Boards. Administrative Procedure Letter No. 4 Re: Giving notice of applications and hearings, recording of decisions, etc.
A.
column2: Notice' of Application:
Application in writing received. If the material in support of the application is not complete, an opportunity to complete it should be given to the applicant.
If application is accompanied by a consent by or on behalf of all parties having any immediate interest in it no notice need be given.
If application is not accompanied by such a consent, the chief executive officer of the board to whom application is made shall give notice as follows;

if the application is made by the employer, to all employees having any immediate interest in it either individually or by posting a form of notice (draft form attached) in the office, plant or works of the employer. The employer may be directed to post such notice for such period and in such manner as the board directs and to furnish proof of the posting;
if the application is made by or on behalf of all employees having any immediate interest in it, to the employer;
if the application is by some but not all employees having any immediate interest in it, to the employer and the other employees who have any immediate interest in it.

In the event that the working conditions in respect of which applications are made are covered by a collective agreement, it will be sufficient if notice to the employees is given to the signatories on their behalf of the collective agreement.

Upon receipt of an application, the chief executive officer will analyse all material submitted with the application and all representations, if any, made in respect thereof and if necessary request further material and make an investigation. A summarized analysis of all material will then be submitted to the board together with any suggestions of the chief executive officer.

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council,QUESTIONS,CANADIANS IN JAPAN,TRANSFER OF PROTECTION OF CANADIAN INTERESTS FROM ARGENTINA TO SWITZERLAND,In accordance with the government's policy of making public as quickly as possible all reliable information received about the welfare of Canadians in enemy hands, a statement about conditions in Hong Kong, received from the British embassy in Chungking, was given to the press last night. It reads:
His Majesty's representative at Chungking reported that he has received information from
Munitions Assignment Board
sources which are considered reasonably reliable concerning the conditions under which Canadian prisoners are being held by the Japanese.

These reports would indicate that Canadians are receiving a good ration of rice supplemented by vegetables and bread daily, and a small quantity of meat. They are allowed to send out their trucks to bring in their food. They are also reported to have their own ovens for baking bread.
The information which has come to hand further discloses that very little disease exists, with the exception of a few cases of dysentery, and that supplies of quinine are on hand in the camp.
From the same reports it would appear that ttinre is a shortage of warm clothing and blankets.

The house is aware that two days ago the Secretary State for Dominion Affairs made a statement in the House of Commons, London, with regard to a decision taken by the United Kingdom, in consultation with the governments of the dominions and of the other united nations, to transfer the protection of British interests in Japan from Argentina to Switzerland.

The welfare of Canadian nationals in Japanese hands, members of the Canadian forces and civilians alike, has been the cause of anxiety to the Canadian government ever since the outbreak of war with Japan. Throughout this trying period the Argentine has been our protecting power in Japan. The Canadian government deeply appreciate the services which have been rendered by the Argentine government, the Argentine foreign office and, in particular, by the Argentine embassy in Tokyo. As a result of their efforts, they have made progress in their work on behalf of Canadian prisoners of war, despite the refusal of the Japanese government to recognize any neutral government as protecting Canadian or British interests in Hong Kong.

Our government's decision to transfer the protection of Canadian interests in Japan from Argentina to Switzerland has been taken in order that the protection of Canadian interests in axis countries should be in the hands of a single protecting power. As Switzerland has assumed the protection of Canadian interests in Germany and Italy, and territories occupied by Germany and Italy, since the United States entered the war, Switzerland has been asked to take over the protection of Canadian interests in Japan. Canadian interests in Japan and Japanese-occupied territories are inextricably bound up with the interests of the United Kingdom and other parts of the Commonwealth, and it is felt that administrative arrangements for their protection can be effectively centralized in a single protecting power.

I may express at least surprise that there should be any question about producing to the house a legal opinion of the Department of Justice on such an important matter of public policy. Heretofore on request I have always been supplied with copies of legal opinions, and perhaps I am not violating any confidence when I say that the minister was good enough to give me this very opinion, though I had no idea that there was any secrecy attached to it. Of course I have not made it public in any way. I think there is an important principle involved. Surely, when the Prime Minister and, I believe, the Minister of National Defence intimate that the government have received such an opinion from the Department of Justice, we ought to know the nature of that opinion. Surely the public are entitled to legal opinions of that kind. I do not think there can be any question about it.

MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Chairman, not often do I claim the attention of this house or of any of its committees. As a matter of fact, if I were to disregard answers to questions, the tabling of returns and other formal occasions of that nature, I could say
War Appropriation-Naval Services

that I have spoken to the house only three times since I have been a member of it, that is, since November, 1940. I have felt that enough speeches were being made on the war without my adding to the number, and I agree with what was said by a newspaper man some months ago that if words could win the war we would have beaten the axis long ago.

It might be of some advantage to the committee if, before any detailed consideration of the estimates of the Department of National Defence for Naval Services be undertaken, I should give to the committee a broad outline of the work of the Royal Canadian Navy. That work is part of the greatest naval undertaking of which history has any record. Every continent in the world, with the exception of south America, is wholly or partly engaged directly in this great struggle. This fact alone implies that men and supplies have to be transported over great distances and that much of that transport has to be over the sea. Five-sevenths of the surface of the earth is covered with water, and since the conflict is now universal or global in character the magnitude of the task of the merchant navies of the allied countries, and of the task of the ships which escort those navies, must be apparent to all.

It is the simple truth to say that if you were to set out by ship from the western shore of Canada across the great Pacific ocean, continue on through the Indian ocean, then around through the Red sea and into the Mediterranean and back into the Atlantic-or you could take the alternative route, down by the island of Madagascar and the cape of Good Hope into the Atlantic-and thence across the Atlantic to the eastern shore of Canada, you would have practically circumnavigated the globe. Over all that tremendous distance, over all that great expanse of water, you would be liable, if you were in a British or allied ship, to attack at any given instant of time. In not a single foot or fathom of those waters could the ship be considered absolutely safe from enemy attack. The allied nations are on the circumference of a great circle, a circle as great as the world; the enemy is within the circle, and he has been and is now able to make sudden thrusts to break the circumference of the circle at any given point. Hence you have thrusts in the Japanese area extending from Australia to the shores of India; you have thrusts by the Germans all along the eastern coast of Europe. It is an easy thing to do; it is a difficult thing to counteract.
Over that 20,000 miles of sea line the ships of the allied countries must ply, carrying men and materials; and where these merchant ships go, escort vesels ought to go also. In the first

years of the war the main line to be guarded was the line running between North America and Great Britain. From the very beginning of the war the Canadian navy has cooperated with the Royal Navy in the defence of that line, and while in recent months the conflict has spread to the Pacific ocean, and, in consequence, other supply routes have to be guarded and maintained, still the Atlantic route, linking Europe and North America, continues to be and always will be of prime importance. That line is now guarded and watched by navies of the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, and it is guarded in almost equal measure by these three navies.

Historically the role of a navy has been to provide battle fleets and to escort merchant ships. The navy's function was to engage the enemy surface craft in direct combat and to protect merchant shipping. Then in the history of naval warfare two new menaces appeared, the mine and the submarine. So that where at one time we needed powerful ships and powerful guns to deal with surface attack, now new methods of naval warfare have to be evolved. These methods take the form of small but fast craft such as destroyers, corvettes, mine-sweepers, motor torpedo boats and smaller types of ships.

It is along these lines that the Canadian navy has developed. Up to the present our navy has been primarily a convoy navy, and its main purpose has been to match in speed and power the attacks made by enemy ships. But as the enemy improves the speed and striking power of his ships we must at the very least keep pace, and desirably we should outstrip him. It is no secret now that some of the enemy U boats, some of the enemy submarines of the more modern type, are considerably faster and stronger than formerly. It is known also that German submarines can leave their bases on the shores of Europe, cross the Atlantic, spend some time hunting ships along the ocean lanes or along the Canadian or United States coasts, and still be able to return to their bases on the shores of Europe without the necessity of refuelling. It is no secret either that submarine attacks have been carried out within sight of the Canadian coast and within sight of the coasts of the United States within recent months.

Our naval engineers here and in the United States and Britain are constantly on the alert to meet these new threats to the safety of our convoy routes. In spite of all that can be done to ovecome submarine attacks it must be admitted that during this year, 1942, merchant shipping losses have been very heavy, particularly in North American coastal waters.

The reason for this condition is to be found in the difficulty of providing convoys for all ships that ply the seas, and the very fact that the enemy has had such a considerable degree of success against non-convoyed ships is proof of the effectiveness of the convoy system. We must provide merchant ships to replace those that have been lost; but, Mr. Speaker, merchant ships alone are helpless to-day, in a war of this character. To the utmost limit of our ability to produce and man them, we and our allies must turn out fighting ships to guard our freighters, our tankers, our supply ships of all kinds that are carrying the products of our farms and factories over the seas. It would be vain and fruitless for us to speed up and greatly increase our production of war supplies for overseas, unless we could transport those supplies overseas. It would be senseless for us to encourage our farmers to produce more and more food for our allies if vre could not carry that food to them.

I come now to the growth of the Canadian navy. I may remind hon. gentlemen that when I first spoke to the House of Commons on naval matters I pointed out that at the beginning of the war the Canadian navy had some fifteen ships available for service; and at the time of my first speech, in November, 1940, I was able to say that this number had increased to 165 ships. At that time I expressed the hope that by the end of the fiscal year 1941-42, that is by last March 31, w'e might reach the figure of 250 ships. I can now say that this figure has been far exceeded, and that at the end of the last fiscal year there were more than 400 ships flying the white ensign and under the command of the Royal Canadian Navy. These ships range from auxiliary cruisers down to destroyers, corvettes, minesweepers, motor patrol boats, motor torpedo boats, and a large number of other auxiliary craft. So that in ships alone the navy to-day is nearly thirty times as great as it was at the outbreak of war.
What about man-power? When the war began the number of men in the navy was 1,774. In late 1940 we planned to have about

column2: men in the navy by the end of the then coming fiscal year, that is, by March 31, 1942. That was our estimate of strength at that time, but that figure too has been well exceeded. Instead of 23,000 men, on that date the Royal Canadian Navy had more than 31,000 men, or an eighteen-fold increase over the figure at the outbreak of war. These men have been enlisted in all parts of Canada. Most of

column1: them have come from the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, of which there are some eighteen divisions in the dominion, from Charlottetown on the east to Vancouver on the west. Every province has given its share of men, though I am bound to say that the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, where the tradition of the sea is strong, have given larger numbers per capita than the other provinces. But as I have said, we have had our share of recruits from all provinces. We have had them from the banks of the St. Lawrence and the Quebec seacoasts, from the shores of the great lakes, from the province of Manitoba, as well as from the prairie provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and there is no lack whatever of recruits for the navy; there is still a very considerable w'aiting list for that service.

Most of our men serve on Canadian ships or in Canadian shore establishments, but more than 1,100 Canadians are serving with the Royal Navy on every type of ship. You will find them in battleships of the British navy, in cruisers, in destroyers, in corvettes, in motor boats, in submarines and in every other type of craft. You will find them on every sea. They have fought in every part of the world-in the Atlantic, in the Pacific, in the Indian ocean and the Mediterranean sea. As a matter of fact when the Royal Navy cruiser Dorsetshire was sunk in the Indian ocean a few weeks ago, no fewer than six of her officers were Canadians, among them the son of my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Fortunately all those young Canadian officers were saved when that ship went down.

The personnel, the man-power of the Canadian navy, depends on several factors. One of these, of course, is the number of men available. In this respect, as I have pointed out, there is no shortage. A second factor is the number of ships. Here for some time the production of ships and the training of men have proceeded at an almost equal pace. But the third factor, which is now beginning to constitute one of the main problems of the navy, is the supply of properly trained officers and petty officers. The training of these men is of necessity, from the very nature of the case, long and varied. They can learn some things on shore, but after they have had all the training that can be given on land there is still a long period of sea training necessary before you have an efficient officer or petty officer. Normally-I am speaking now of peace time-a man would not be given command of a ship unless he had served for some years at a school or shore establishment, then
War Appropriation-Naval Services

a period of service at sea, then, more time on shore, and then again to sea as a junior officer. In the British navy in normal times it would take a man from twelve to fourteen years, from the time he entered the navy as a youth, before he would be considered fit to command a ship. In war time of course there are many cases in which that time has to be considerably abridged. But with a navy such as ours, which at the beginning of the war had only 1,774 officers and men, it can be seen how difficult was the task and how difficult is the task to-day of providing from so small a nucleus for the expansion which has taken place.

We have been fortunate in having in the country a large number of professional seamen, men who manned our fishing fleets and our mercantile marine, on our great rivers and lakes, and on both oceans. Many of these men have found their way into the navy, and have been of invaluable assistance. But in spite of that, and desirable as that accretion to our strength has been, we have had to rely for our personnel mainly on men who have had no great amount of training in ships. The bulk of our personnel has come from the civilian population-from the clerks, the labourers, the doctors, the lawyers and business men of our cities, towns, villages and hamlets. But just as the Canadian army in the last war was made up largely of this sort of men, and just as that army acquitted itself with such gallantry on the battlefields of Europe, so, I am sure, will the Canadian navy, recruited in much the same manner, continue to prove worthy of itself and of Canada.

Perhaps I should say a word to the committee about naval training. The training of naval ratings, the men on the lower decks, in the ranks, is begun ordinarily at one or other of our eighteen volunteer reserve divisions. At these divisions the rating receives preliminary disciplinary training for a period of about eight weeks. He is then transferred from the division to a coastal area, either on the east or west coast, and he receives there what is called ""new entry training."" This training lasts for a period of ten weeks. Following this he is drafted to sea. After he has his sea legs he may be brought ashore for more highly specialized training, such as training in gunnery', torpedo work, wireless or anti-submarine work. I may say that every effort is put forth by our officers and petty officers to place technical and skilled men at the kind of work where their qualifications will produce the best results. So much for the training of ratings.
Now to the training of officers. This is usually undertaken in the first instance at one of the volunteer reserve divisions. The prospective officer attaches himself to one or other

of these divisions, and undergoes a certain amount of training there. In due course he will be interviewed by a selection board of naval officers who decide whether or not he is likely to become an efficient naval officer. If the decision is yes, he is then called to an officers' training establishment at Esquimalt or Halifax, where he is given a four months' course. During that time he is known as a probationary' sub-lieutenant. If he is successful in his course he drops the term ""probationary'"" and becomes a sub-lieutenant, and is assigned to duty either on a ship or in some shore establishment.

I believe the committee will be glad to know -and it is indicative of the very high calibre of the men we have been able to attract to the ranks of the naval service-that no fewer than 512 of the men who entered as ratings, in the ranks, have been promoted to officer ranks since the beginning of the war. Officers in command of ships, and all others charged with the supervision of men, are constantly on the alert to discover among those under their command those qualities of initiative, courage, leadership and resourcefulness necessary for good officer material. There is no bar to advancement in the navy, except the bar of inefficiency.

There are one or two further matters in connection with training which I shall mention. In addition to the training we undertake ourselves directly, in the divisions and at the posts, we have also taken advantage of various training schemes arranged throughout the country to qualify young men in the mechanical trades. The navy has now some 700 young men who have entered upon courses which will last for approximately three years, and which will qualify them for positions as artificers skilled in engine room, electrical and other types of mechanical work. These young men begin the course at about the age of seventeen years; and in due time they will form a reservoir of well-trained, technical men who will be available for the naval service.

In this connection I would point out that several universities across the country have helped us greatly by training naval technicians, particularly in radio and anti-submarine work. With the development of scientific warfare, and with the increasing complexity of its instruments, technical training has become increasingly important. It has been said, and said truly, that a ship to-day is not only a ship; it is an arsenal and a floating machine shop as well.
We require skilled mechanics on ships. We also require skilled mechanics in naval dock yards for the purpose of repairing the ships.
War Appropriation-Naval Services

I am sure I need not emphasize the importance of prompt and efficient repair work. A fighting ship is of no value whatever tied to a dock. If she is damaged she must be repaired as quickly as possible and made ready for sea again. Some of this work of course can be done in private yards; but the naval dock yards must be prepared to do their full share. With that in view it may be necessary to increase the establishment at these dock yards.

Not only do we have to consider repairs in our yards, but we have to take account of new inventions which seek to counteract or to anticipate the tactics of our enemies. We have to incorporate these in our ships from time to time, if the ships and their crews are not to be placed at a serious disadvantage. I am happy to say that so far as repairs to ships are concerned, the work carried on in Canadian yards is done in approximately the same time and with the same skill as is shown in the yards of the United States and the United Kingdom.

A new type of service on which the navy is about to embark is to be provided by the women's corps. Like the army and the air force, the naval service feels that there are many posts and positions now being filled by men which could be filled equally well by women, and that immediately new posts arise, they should be filled by women. Accordingly, we propose to establish a women's branch of the service similar to the Women's Royal Naval Service, or ""Wrens"", as they are called in Great Britain. Some leading members of the British women's service will arrive shortly in Canada to assist in the organization of the branch here. When the organization is fully under way it is expected that several thousand Canadian women will be incorporated into the new branch.

1266480,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.7,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Administrative work and the like. I should like to say that there are women's auxiliaries which in many cases have attached themselves to branches of the naval volunteer reserve divisions throughout the country. These have done a fine work, all voluntary of course, in providing comforts in the way of

clothing, reading matter and the like for men at sea. What these women from one end of Canada to the other have done is fully appreciated by the men who have to brave the rigours of the north Atlantic winter. I know they will always remember with profound gratitude the interest and the support of these women's auxiliaries.

Another organization to which I should like to refer is the Navy League of Canada, whose work, particularly on behalf of merchant seamen, has been of great importance and great value. These men are out in all kinds of weather and in all seasons, in the cold of winter and in the heat of summer; their calling is dangerous enough in peace time, but is trebly dangerous now, and anything that can be done for them is well deserved. The navy league has given particular attention to these gallant merchant seamen. It has built hostels in coastal ports and in ports on the St. Lawrence river; it has provided clothing and other comforts for men in many parts of Canada, not only for Canadian merchant seamen, but the seamen of our allied friends as well. The navy league has' always taken a special interest in the sea cadets. Last summer the Canadian navy decided to assume fuller responsibility for the sea cadets, and we secured the services of Mr. R. C. Stevenson of Montreal to act as coordinator of sea cadet activities. He is responsible to the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, but he works in close association with the navy league. I may say that there are now 2.700 sea cadets in Canada who range in age from twelve to eighteen years. By the end of the present fiscal year we hope that that number will be increased to some 8,000. We have found from experience that many young men who have had training as sea cadets have been able to shorten considerably the training time ordinarily consumed by new entries into the navy. Many of our best officers and ratings have had training with the sea cadet corps.

One word about the medical services of [DOT]the navy. I may say to the committee that we now have 170 doctors and some 40 nurses in the Royal Canadian Navy. Forty doctors are with the Royal Navy, so that the total number administering to our own personnel is 130 doctors. I am glad to be able to say that the health of the navy is good. In

column2: hospital days there have been 23 deaths from illness. Recruits for the navy show a high standard of health; for only 10-3 per cent of those who apply for enlistment have had to be rejected, and after enlistment only about 3 per cent of the personnel have had to be discharged on medical grounds.

column1: War Appropriation-Naval Services

The naval service also carries on very extensive research work, some of it under the direction of eminent medical men in this country. Among these I might mention Doctor C. H. Best of Toronto, whose research work with Doctor Banting in the field of insulin brought him international fame. He is now a naval officer, and he and many others are giving their attention to the study of diets on board ship and on shore, even to the study of seasickness, to the study of conditions which affect the eyesight of men, to the problem of the fatigue among technical operators, to the effect of noise on men's nerves and the possibility of eliminating it, and so on.

I think the committee knows in a general way what the duties of the Royal Canadian Navy are. I have often said that they are threefold. In the first place, they guard the coasts of Canada; in the second place, they escort convoys across the seas, and, in the third place, they take aggressive action against the enemy whenever possible. All these three functions very often merge one into the other. For example, if a Canadian vessel is escorting a convoy across the Atlantic and attacks and destroys a German submarine on the way, she is discharging all three functions at once. She is, of course, escorting and protecting her convoy, she is guarding the coasts of Canada by destroying an enemy vessel, and she is also taking aggressive action against the enemy. I think it would be correct to say that up to the present the task of convoying ships has been the main task of the Canadian navy. In a war of this kind the convoying of ships is a matter of the greatest importance. The task of carrying food and other supplies from Canada across the seas falls to the merchant navies of the united nations, and the task of escorting those merchant ships falls to the battle craft of the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada.

Our navy, consisting of a goodly number of small craft such as destroyers and corvettes, is peculiarly suited to the task of convoying. That was the work which we were asked to undertake at the beginning of the war; that was the work that lay nearest to our hand and that is the work we have continued to do for the past two and one-half years. How important that work is to the success of the common cause will appear readily when I say that since the beginning of this war more than 56 million tons of cargo have been carried from these shores across the Atlantic, and that more than 9,000 ships have been convoyed over those waters. I exclude from

those figures, of course, troop convoys which have also left our shores and which have had gratifying good luck in their voyages. The work of the convoy has all the dangers of sea warfare-the submarine, the mine, the surface raider, the enemy aircraft-in addition to ordinary perils of waters. All these dangers have to be braved to-day by the men who go down to the sea in ships, and more than five hundred members of the Royal Canadian Navy have given their lives since the outbreak of the war. Seventy-two honours and decorations have been awarded to our personnel.

A word as to our plans for the future of the navy. In the present fiscal year we hope to enlarge our personnel by some 13,000 officers and men. In other words, I hope that by March 31, 1943, the Canadian navy will have a strength of about 44,000, and in the same time I hope we can add not far, from 100 ships to our fleet.

Another thing I should mention is the opening of the naval college at Esquimalt, on the west coast of Canada, in September or October of this year. I think everyone will now agree that the closing of the old naval college which was first established at Halifax in 1910 was a most unfortunate occurrence. I have already told the committee something of the difficulty that we experience in providing trained officers and petty officers, and this difficulty has been greatly aggravated by the fact that since 1923 no naval college has existed in this country. It is my fervent hope that this naval college, once established, will be continued forever and will become a training ground for men seeking to adopt naval life as a profession, whether as officers of the Canadian navy or in the mercantile marine. I hope also that after this war Canada will resume and even enhance her position as one of the great trading nations of the world, sending her goods to all parts of the world; and if that is to be so, we must have in this country an establishment wherein men to man Canadian ships can be fully trained.

It is only thirty-two years since the foundations of the Canadian navy were laid. Indeed, many of the men w:ho were Canada's first naval cadets and recruits are still on active service. It is a new navy; in comparison to the sea forces of other great nations it must be called a small navy; but it is shaping its own traditions of valour and service, and it draws much of its inspiration from the Royal Navy itself.
I wonder if there is in any country a fighting service that has had so long, so important and so glorious a place in that country's history as the British navy. Its record goes
War Appropriation-Naval Services

back almost to the beginnings of the nation; for the people of Britain realized early that a strong navy was absolutely essential to the defence of their island. The pageant of British naval achievement is great and colourful, and in it at one time or another are to be found some of the great names of England. Drake the Devon man, is there, and Hawkins and Howard and Blake, and Sir Richard Grenville of the Revenge, and Rooke and Rodney and Frobisher and Raleigh and Collingwood; and above them all the towering figure of Nelson himself. They are joined in this war by a great and goodly company: by the men of Montevideo, by the naval heroes of Narvik, by the gallant Captain Fogarty Fegen, of the Jervis Bay, going to certain death to protect his convoy; by those men who stayed in their ships off the coast of Crete under terrible naval and air attack and who, suffering grievously as they were, nevertheless made good their promise that no German troops would be landed on that island by sea. They are joined by the men who fought against overwhelming odds in Malaya and at other points in the far east; by the men of Dunkirk, where the seamen of England, the fighting ships of England, the merchant ships, the yachts, the tugs, and the motor boats rescued 335,000 troops from irreparable disaster. It has been well said of the British navy by a Britisher:

Theirs is a great imperial service, a service whose tradition is silence, whose devotion to duty is as unobtrusive as it is instinctive, the graves of whose heroes are recorded neither in brass nor in stone, for they lie in every latitude, in the fathomless depths of the unplumbed, salt, estranging sea.

It is with that service, Mr. Chairman and hon. members of the committee, that the young Canadian navy has the honour to be associated. It is in that service that many of our officers and men have been trained. It is the traditions of that service that we take as our own.

There are some, I know, in the world to-day who look back into history and who raise their eyes from the record to tell a dismal tale of Britain's mistakes and England's misdeeds in the past. Let us admit that she has made mistakes, as what nation has not? What shield is without its shadow? But for my part, as I have said elsewhere, admitting errors and recognizing faults, I take my stand on the words of a Greek statesman, spoken twenty-five centuries ago, ""For even when life's previous record shows faults and failures, it is just to weigh the last brave hour of devotion against them all."" And against all the mistakes, all the injustices, all the faults of their country's past, I set the heroic stand of the British people in these times, their stand

for world freedom, justice, order and decency, and I await with complete confidence the tilt of the scale. The main burden of enemy attack has been borne by the island of Britain for two and a half years. For two and a half years she has had to experience the most ruthless sort of warfare. Her lanes of commerce have been savagely attacked. Her cities and her countryside have been blackened by enemy bombs. ' Her people, young and old, have experienced the full force and horror of war. Yet she bears herself gallantly, this nursery of freedom, this mother of democracy. She draws on her deep reservoirs of courage and tradition. She kindles the imagination of the present with the torch of the past. She appeals not in vain to the great exploits of other days and her seamen remember the tradition of Drake. Drake dying ordered his drum to be taken to England, declaring that if ever the country stood in dire peril they should beat it and he would come back from his grave.
Take my drum to England, hang it by the shore,
Strike it when your powder's runnin' low.
If the Dons sight Devon, I'll quit the port o' Heaven,
An' drum them up the Channel as we drummed them long ago.
In that setting, Mr. Chairman, in that background, the Royal Canadian Navy proceeds to its task and moves forward to its destiny.

1266481,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.8,1942-05-07,4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1,ca.m.6010,Mr. STIRLING:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I feel sure that the members of the committee have listened with deep attention and very great interest to the account which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has given of the affairs of his department. He has touched on the very close association which exists between the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Navy. He has referred to the fact that the Royal Canadian Navy draws its officers and men from all the provinces of Canada through certain channels, and it has always appeared to me that we must never omit the expression of gratitude to those who in the earlier days of the Royal Canadian Navy laid plans so well that those plans have been successful in doing exactly what they were intended to do.

I do not go back to the years before the great war. Canada has a naval history beginning then. I refer rather to what happened after the great war, after Canadians of all ages and ranks had served with the Royal Navy for the common purpose. After the great war, when we were settling down into a period of idealism, when we were wading through idealism, and setting up for ourselves ideals that unfortunately have not been attained, plans were laid to maintain
War Appropriation-Naval Services

a navy for Canada. It was realized that the way which it might be possible to follow would be to create and to maintain a small permanent force, and it has only been with great difficulty on many occasions that that little Canadian navy has been preserved. For again and again, through those years of peace, there were those in this house and in the public press who endeavoured to belittle the efforts which went to maintain the Royal Canadian Navy. Still it survived, because fortunately successive governments realized that it would not be reasonable to destroy that little naval germ which had been established with so much difficulty in Canada.

That was what one might call the first part of the plan. The second part was to make arrangements for the provision and then the training of those who should enter the Canadian navy. That was a twofold effort: the Royal Canadian Volunteer Reserve, to which the minister has alluded, and the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, to which he has also referred, explaining that it was formed from those whose wrork takes them on the sea in the ordinary way in the merchant navy.

I think it is a remarkable thing that the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, created at a time when Commodore Hose, now Admiral, was chief of the naval staff, and created so that there should be representatives of it in all the provinces of Canada, should have been so successful in retaining the interests of Canadians. For although two of the provinces do not. touch salt water, and three others touch it but very little, yet we find that through the interest and the call of the navy, the attraction, history, whatever may be the reason, through all these the Royal Canadian naval volunteer reserves have been successful in keeping up the stream when the pressure of war has come, so that to-day the minister is able, in the third year of the war, to describe the extraordinary increase both in numbers and in tonnage in what was once this little naval germ in Canada.

Of course, the retention of the permanent force, small though it was, was only possible because of the training which was available to our young officers and petty officers in their close connection with the Royal Navy. Our cadets, our midshipmen and sublieutenants took their early training in the Royal Navy. Our vessels were not numerous enough or large enough to give them experience. It was necessary for them to be with the Royal Navy. Ever since the creation of the Royal Canadian Navy these junior officers have gone to the Royal Navy and received the training, yes, and the traditions, beaten deep into them

from association with the Royal Navy. Our gunners, our torpedo men, our signallers and petty officers have gone there and received instruction and they with our young officers on their return have imparted that instruction and assisted in the training of what has now grown to the very considerable naval effort of Canada.

I should like the minister to give us a great deal of information in expansion of the bare outline which he did give. I think, if I may say so, he did wisely in touching on a good number of points connected with the navy, but perhaps we had better take them one by one. He might deal with two or three that occur to my mind on which I think we should like to have some information. In the first place the estimated figure for this financial year, is, I believe, $269,000,000. I believe that is S120,000,000 greater than the corresponding figure for last year. Last year the minister divided that into a considerable number of headings. We should like him on this occasion also to divide the amount up, indicating as he goes where the principal increases have gone.

Then with regard to training, the references which he made in his speech appeared to me to cover principally the training which is afforded to the officers and men of the volunteer reserve. I should like also to know what the state of the Royal Canadian Navy entry is. So far as I am aware we are still receiving boy entry and we are still receiving cadet entry both for executive and for pay. I should like him to tell us whether the routine of peace days has in any way been departed from in the training which they receive. For instance, do our cadets go over and receive similar cruiser training to that which they received when the Frobisher was the training cruiser?

With regard to the training of the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, the minister referred to the first lot of training and the second lot of training which took place at the sea coasts. I should like him to amplify that and give us detailed description of the training establishments which must of necessity have been set up on both coasts to provide for that training; and also to tell us, on the question of training, with regard to those who enter from the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, the merchant service and the fishing' boats, whether those officers and men also receive refresher courses before they go to sea in the corvettes and the like.

1266482,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.9,1942-05-07,85a45525-d20a-41db-8c2a-1b91c360656b,ca.m.7972,Mr. COLDWELL:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Wre have listened to an interesting outline this afternoon, similar in some respects to the information which was given us on another occasion. I am sure
War Appropriation-Naval Services

every hon. member of this house feels a debt of gratitude to the men who are serving in the navy and in the merchant marine, and anyone who speaks at this time, as the minister did himself and the hon. member for Yale a few moments ago, cannot but appreciate the tremendous place which the navy holds in the minds of all our people and the task which it performs in the great struggle in which we are now engaged.

I was interested in hearing the minister recite ""Drake's Drum""; for as a boy I was brought up in the district in which that legend originated, in the land of the men to whom he has referred, the men of Devon; great as are the traditions of the navy, those who at this time are engaged in convoying or in operating the merchant ships are perhaps engaged in an even more difficult and dangerous task than that of the men of ancient times who sailed the oceans and brought their ships in safety to the shores of new distant continents.

The hon. member for Yale was asking some questions about training and the establishments that have been set up for training the personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy. I have no doubt the minister will give those answers in a little while. It is interesting to note that many of the men who have joined the navy in recent months came from the prairies, from regions where there is little water, and many a young naval lad's first sight of the sea was the day he began to take training at one of the coasts or on a ship. That they have made good seamen goes without comment, because we have heard it on every hand. When we were in Great Britain we met at Portsmouth some of our Canadian boys who were serving in the Royal Navy, and had an opportunity of chatting with them about their experiences. I wish to take this opportunity, when discussing the personnel of the navy and their training, to express the hope-I am not the first to raise the question; it has been brought up by other hon. members on both sides of the house- that the pay and particularly the allowances to the dependents of our naval men will be increased. Only at noon to-day the wife of an officer who is looking after wives of men who are serving, not in the navy but in the air force, was telling me of the really deplorable conditions under which some of the wives and families of our naval men are living in Montreal and in other Canadian ports. It is a blot upon this country that the allowances to the men engaged in such a difficult and dangerous task are so much less than those given to men in the army or the air force. I would not of course have it underfMr. Cold well.]

stood that I think the allowances made to the dependents of men who serve in the army and the air force are at all adequate in these days of increased costs of living. That they are inadequate serves only to emphasize the point I am making, that the wife of a man serving in the navy, and receiving $15 a month less than the wife of a man serving in the army or the air force, has to live upon a standard that is impossibly low at any time but more particularly in these days of high prices.

I am glad to know that the number of our ships is being increased so rapidly. I realize of course that many of them are small ships. I recall that before the war broke out our friend and colleague at that time, Mr. Grant MacNeil, then the member for Vancouver North, often spoke in this house on the necessity of obtaining fast small boats for coastal patrol work. That policy is being carried out to a degree to-day. And if I may say so, the very fact that we are building many corvettes and many smaller boats and that we have so many of our young men serving in these small ships, is another reason why we should give every consideration to the conditions ashore under which the men and their families live. Those of us who have been on mine-sweepers, or corvettes know very well that the quarters are cramped; the ships are small, and on the stormy Atlantic to live on one of those boats must be indeed uncomfortable to say the least. Everything this house and the government can do to make conditions as favourable as possible for the men who go down to the sea in ships, both of the Royal Canadian Navy and the merchant service, ought to be done. I was brought up by the sea, and have often seen the ships of the Royal Navy anchored in the bay. In Canada I have seen our ships at Halifax in winter time. I realize that difficult and, in bad weather, dirty as the job was along the coasts of Britain, and particularly along the shores of the English channel, it was not comparable to the difficulties and discomforts which the men of our Atlantic coast, in particular, have to undergo. When I saw ships coming into Halifax almost encased in ice I marvelled at the courage and fortitude of the men who had to withstand not only the mighty waves of the ocean but the frigid cold of winter on the Atlantic coast. And when we think that during the past few months they have helped to convoy hundreds of thousands of tons of shipping and supplies across the sea, not only to the beleagured island of Britain but also to our allies in Russia, to our troops in Africa and now across the Pacific ocean, facing not only the dangers of the weather but also torpedoes, bombings from
War Appropriation-Naval Services

the air and every devilish device which the ingenuity of man has brought to bear in this great war, we cannot but marvel at their courage. So I say that anything we can do to improve conditions for the men while they are at sea, to provide proper recreational facilities for them when they come ashore in the great ports, and to provide adequately for their families, should be done. I am not going to repeat what I have said so often about Halifax, but we should see that the wives and families of these men are properly housed and provided for.

The matter of housing accommodation is one into which I think the department should look very carefully, and which I think should be strictly supervised by the rent control authorities. I refer to the rent that has to be paid by these seamen-yes, and this applies to the air force and to the men in the army, to some extent-who from time to time have to move with their families from place to place, who have to find new quarters and who therefore are not always protected by the rent restrictions which protect those of us who have been located in the one place for the past two or three years. We should see that these men are not victimized through being charged high rents in the various cities and ports to which they have to move.

As this discussion proceeds I have no doubt that the minister will be asked a great many questions with regard to our ships and our men, and as to the conditions under which those ships operate and the men serve. I do not propose to ask any questions now, but we as a group have some questions in mind which my colleagues and I will be asking as the question period progresses. However, I do want to take this first opportunity of urging upon the government the necessity of seeing to it that these men are remunerated-not properly, because money cannot properly remunerate them-to an extent more nearly commensurate with their services, and that at least their wives and dependents are protected to a far greater degree than they are a>t present. The other afternoon I said some-. thing about the delinquency in Toronto among the children of men overseas and women working in factories. I understand that the same condition exists in Montreal and other seaport and industrial cities. As I said then, each of our defence departments should see to it that the government and the treasury board are made aware of the requirements, so that a suitable appropriation may be made in order that the children of the men and women who serve may be well looked after by the communities in which they live. That will require federal grants and appropriations.

We may be proud of the part that has been played already by the small Royal Canadian Navy, which is expanding month by month. I think we owe a debt, as a parliament and as a nation, to the men who are serving us in many capacities in that navy and in the merchant service of our own and the allied countries.

1266483,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.10,1942-05-07,2db22441-d3ea-4e76-8d18-f4753949bd74,ca.m.812,Mr. BLACKMORE:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Mr. Chairman, since the beginning of this war I have derived a great deal of satisfaction from the fact that this country has given so much attention to the navy, and has recognized the necessity for increasing it. I can remember as a small *boy wondering why Canada, with the resources which should enable her to build a great navy, should limp along so helplessly in this regard in the great British commonwealth of nations. The history of the British empire and the British people has been intimately and inextricably bound up with the sea, with ships. For over a thousand years the Britishh navy has been supreme, until it has become a tradition, almost an instinct, on the part of British people to expect that their fleet should be able to conquer any other fleet or any combination of other fleets that might be brought against it. Why Canada did not build a powerful and efficient supplement to the British navy, I never could make out.

I welcome the report of the minister indicating that our navy is expanding. There is quite a tendency on the part of many people to believe that when this war is over we are going to emerge automatically into a new order in which we no longer will be called upon to defend ourselves. Judged by all history and all common sense, Mr. Chairman, ideas of that sort are utter nonsense. We should build permanently, build deep and strong, and build for the future. Perhaps men will be able to organize a giant, superworld-state under the canopy or wings of which all nations may be able to rest quiescent, but I see no evidence of it. I should say the first thing for us to 'do is to be strong. If a great super-state should be built up willing and able to guard the peace and safety of the world, that will be the time to relax our efforts toward making ourselves secure, but certainly we should not do so before such a state has been evolved. We are going, I fancy, into an era of great tribulation. Probably the most -war-like time in all the world's history stretches before us within the next generation. I believe the minister and his department should have this in mind, so that they may not build temporarily. They ought not to cease to build when the war is over, but should prepare themselves for an era of perhaps fifty years during every one of which
War Appropriation-Naval Services
the ships of Canada and the men of Canada shall be ready and able to go forth upon the seas and meet any enemy which may come.

There will be those who will wonder how Canada could sustain such a programme financially. With that aspect of the question I am not going to deal, except briefly to point out, as has been stated many times already, that what is physically possible can be made financially possible. The number of ships Canada can build and man will depend upon the iron., coal, timber and other necessities for the building of ships which can be found in Canada. It will depend, too, upon the number of men and factories which can be found to build the ships, and the number of men who can man the ships. Let us adopt a progressive policy, one which values children; and I think we shall have no difficulty in raising sufficient Canadians through the years to come, to man and to build as large ships and as many ships as we need.

I should like to add my voice to those who have contended that better pay should be given to those in the navy. We should make the navy attractive not only romantically but economically. I feel that the men who join our forces, whether the army, the navy or the air force, should move among us as select men, as the elite. I see no reason why they should be paid an income so small that they are fearful of the future or, shall I say, hesitant about living generously in the present. I believe it is possible for Canada to provide all her fighting men with all the needs of life, not only while the war endures, but just as long after the war as they shall live.

It is a most shortsighted and destructive policy on our part to neglect the possibilities of the children of our fighting forces. There is no reason why there should not be a good family for every man in the fighting forces, and no reason why anyone should hesitate to marry and to rear' children because- of financial circumstances and anxieties. We would all grant that those who join the fighting forces are the noblest among us. They are strong; they are courageous; they are healthy. Surely they should be the parents of the generation to come. I would urge upon the minister that he do everything in his power to make it possible for every one of the men under his direction to have a good home, a good family and complete confidence in his economic future.

1266485,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.12,1942-05-07,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Mr. Chairman, as honorary president of the Navy League of Canada, Ontario division, I would be derelict in my duty on behalf of that body if I were not to rise at the earliest opportunity and thank the minister for his very kind references to the work that has been and is being done by that organization. I do so with very great pleasure. What has amazed me since Canada first began to take part in this sea warfare has been the record of the achievements of our various ships. They have done splendidly even though they are not large. Our men have given evidence of being as brave and of possessing as much fortitude as the men in any other fleet. On reading the names of those who have suffered or who have been lost, I have been amazed to see the number who came from the provinces remote from the sea, especially the western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Later when the minister is ready to give us some figures I should like to have the number who have enlisted from each province. All reports about fighting on the sea have recorded the conspicuous gallantry of these young men. We should expect of those who were born near the sea a love of the sea and a willingness to render excellent sea service, but the record has been the same of those who come from my own province of Ontario and from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. It gives a clear indication and example that fortitude and strength and heroism are not confined only to people living close to the sea.

Like others who have spoken, I have been pleased with the expansion in our naval forces as outlined by the minister. In this connection I was glad to hear what the minister said about the personnel of our ships. As he said, there is no use in having ships unless we have the personnel to man them. I believe I first became associated with the navy league in 1917, the year it was founded. A famous man from Portsmouth, one of the great union heads, came here; I believe his name was Peter Wright. He had performed a great work in keeping up the morale of the people in the old country, and he brought with him the same high spirit. I met him on several occasions and I was always thrilled by his bravery.

The navy league has done a splendid work. There are sea cadet corps right across Canada, commencing in Vancouver, then Calgary, Regina and a most excellent corps in Winnipeg. In its day, if it was not the strongest numerically it was certainly one of the best trained corps in Canada. At the head of the lakes there were corps at Fort William and Sault Ste. Marie. Then there was an outstanding and very strong corps at Toronto. This was the headquarters for Ontario as well as the principal branch of the Navy League of Canada. In Ontario there were corps at Welland, London, Kingston, and Ottawa, as well as at Montreal, Quebec, Saint John, New Brunswick, and Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. Tl'.ere was also an excellent organization at Halifax.

I often think of the splendid men and women who gave their time freely to this work. The women tried to make things comfortable for the boys around headquarters and in the different towns and cities. They provided comforts of one kind and another and occasionally a dinner to encourage the young lads. I think of the men who trained them. The amazing thing to me is that there were so many men who were willing to give of their time and means, particularly of their time, in training these young lads in the way they should go. In years gone by when the present Minister of Pensions and National Health, at that time minister of defence, would bring down the estimates for cadet training I never failed to support them. It always surprised me that there were members in this house who bitterly opposed voting money for this most laudable work of training young men. Cadet training taught them to be civil, to be courteous, to be manly, to do the very things that are so much required to-day by young men in our navy. I thank the minister sincerely for his kindly remarks about the Navy League of Canada and for his support of the league since he became minister.

It may be a little early to suggest it, but I do suggest to the minister that some plan be initiated by the department of naval services to provide some means of living or some plan of living after the war for the thousands of men now in the naval service. The minister has told us that there are some

column2: in the service, with the number constantly increasing until we may reach perhaps

or 50,000. Many of these young men never worked at anything else in their lifetime ; their only training has been in the naval service. Many of them came from the farms of the west or Ontario, and when they leave the service they will know nothing about the problems of life outside the service. I hope the minister will start now to consider

column1: War Appropriation-Naval Services
some plan under which thousands of these fine naval personnel can be placed in permanent positions after the war.

After the last war I went to England as a member of a delegation to interview Lord Jellicoe, who at that time was head of the colonization service, if not of all England in any event of the Anglican church. I was greatly interested in the keen grasp that that great man had of the need of doing something for the thousands of men who had served under him at Jutland and under other admirals during the great war. As a result of that meeting the navy league was successful in placing here in Canada several thousands of those wonderful men; I have just forgotten the exact number. Many of them were placed on farms, and at that time the navy league made it its business to keep in contact with the men who had been placed as a result of the work of Lord Jellicoe and his committee. On many occasions it was my great delight to visit some of these families and observe how they were getting along. They made good. That type of man could not do anything else but make good. I hope the minister will proceed at once to initiate some plan to take care of the personnel of the Canadian navy after the war.

I can remember the bitter debate that took place in this house at the time the naval college was closed. I hope that never again will this parliament have to listen to such tirades as were delivered on that occasion against the men who were interested in maintaining the strength of this empire. I do not blame only those who were in the house at that time; I blame also the pacifists outside the house. Any man who advocated a vote for the sea cadets or for the maintenance of our military institutions was branded a warmonger. I am glad to say that that is all past. Nobody to-day would have the unfairness to charge supporters of the maintenance of our defence institutions with war-monger-ing. But, Mr. Chairman, this empire would not be in the difficulty it is in to-day, and many thousands of the gallant men of our empire would not now lie dead in Malaya, in the oceans and elsewhere had not dear old England too succumbed to much the same kind of pacifist talk that we in this House of Commons had to endure, and that had such an effect on the estimates of the then Minister of National Defence, now the Minister of Pensions and National Health. I was always glad to support him against such attacks, and on many occasions urged him to increase the grants for cadet training. It is too bad that that was not done.
May I now pay a tribute to another part of the group which constitutes our naval

strength; I refer to the men back in the factories-workmen, designers, draftsmen, machinists, riveters, and those who organized the plants for the building of ships. On many occasions in past years I have heard those who operate these plants denounced in this chamber as being everything they should not be. Yet I do not know what this country or Great Britain would do to-day without the men who in years gone by erected plants and factories and organized their businesses to produce what we are making to-day. Reflect on what this country has done since the war broke out. It is a matter for wonder what the artisans in our factories and the men who operate the factories have done. As the minister has said, they have increased the number of Canadian ships from 15 in 1939 to over 400 at the present time. This result reflects great credit on all Canadians engaged in the making and operating of ships; I might even add that it is creditable to the humble man on the street whom we hear calling ""Rags, bones, scrap iron"", men who gather waste materials. Scrap iron is cutting a big figure in this war. It is by far the most important part of the iron used in steel plate. The men who are working down the iron mines are doing a wonderful job; my heart warms to them, because many a time I have been in the iron mines, and I know they deserve great praise. But without scrap iron it would be difficult to turn out steel with the rapidity with which it is being produced to-day.

1266487,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.14,1942-05-07,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,That is true. Those who have knowledge of the achievements of engine factories, without whose product, of course, our ships could not operate, must be proud of what Canadian plants are doing. The Canadian Allis-Chalmers company, a tremendously large concern with branches in several cities of the dominion, has a very large plant located partly in my own riding and partly in that of the hon. member for High Park. It is currently turning out the 1,200 horse-power engines, one each week, which are required to propel corvettes. I am happy to salute with all my heart the men engaged in producing engines in Canada, from the lowliest worker in these great plants to the men in the highest positions. I am happy to say further, from my close connection with many plants, that the majority of the head men in these large institutions came right up from the humblest ranks in the plant. That is a great tribute to the opportunities given to the Canadian worker to advance and the advantage he takes of those opportunities.
War Appropriation-Naval Services

I would not omit a reference to the men in the mines of Quebec-at Asbestos, I believe. What could we do without the men who produce the asbestos which not only covers pipes but provides material for the apparel which sailors to-day have to wear to withstand the flames of bombs if they should be unfortunate enough to be on a ship on which bombs fall. The asbestos miner deserves credit too.
Ours is a great country. Every Canadian may well be proud not only of those who man the ships but of those who make the ships.

The minister could, I know, have gone much further than he did in telling of what has been achieved. In making his statement he displayed an eloquence which few men possess, and a power of expression which carries conviction. He could have told us much more about what our men are doing; but, having done it before, I assume he thought it unnecessary to say more about their work in the guarding of convoys, in which I believe that five hundred lost their lives-heroes, every one of them.

Some days ago I went to offer my sympathy to the mother of a young man who lost his life in the sinking of the Spikenard, one of our ships from which, I believe, only seven were saved. It would thrill anyone to talk to a heroine like that lady. Her courage, her realization that her boy had made the supreme sacrifice for the maintenance of this empire, exemplifies the spirit which will save the empire. I am one of those who believe that we shall win the war in spite of everything, because our people continue to display the courage which their forefathers have shown down through the ages. I read this boy's last letter to his mother, written from England. It was a fine letter, indicative of the kind of bringing up he had had. His mother's words were always in his mind. It mattered not to him what might happen; he was serving, he believed, in the highest cause to which a man could devote himself. His chum, I believe one of the seven who were saved, later sent a cablegram which showed the unflinching spirit of the boys on the ship. It was addressed to this heroic mother, formerly Mrs. Walker, now Mrs. T. W. Cartmill, living at 117 Lappin Avenue, Toronto, and it read:
Regret Sammy went down with his ship.

Sammy Walker was his name. Well, that is a British tradition, to go down with the ship. That is what Admiral Tom Phillips did on the Prince of Wales out there east of Malaya. It is a British tradition, to go down with the ship and not to run away from it-fighting with the ship to the last, and then, if necessary, going down with it. That is the British spirit.

I might add one word to what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) said in reference to pay and allowances, because from Toronto quite a number of men have enlisted in the navy and many times men have come to me asking why their pay and allowances are not the same as the pay and allowances in the army. I do not know what the rates are, so I cannot speak from knowledge of any comparison, but if they are not paid on equal terms I know the minister will do anything that is necessary to improve the situation.

There was another matter that came to my attention. I am not sure of the facts, but my memory is that if the commander of a ship in Halifax, say, was moved to Victoria he would have to pay his own way out. The minister shakes his head. I am glad to know that has been changed, because that would be manifestly unfair.

And now a last word with regard to recreation on shore. The minister knows there is a bit of conflict going on in Halifax in connection with some club. I am not familiar with the particulars, but I believe, as I think the minister does-and every other hon. member believes it too-that the finest and most comfortable places should be provided for men when they come ashore from their ships. While I am not a drinking man myself- I have never tasted liquor, so that it means nothing to me personally-I realize that many of these men do like a glass of liquor or a glass of beer. It is their business whether they take it or not, and all I say is this. I ask the minister to make certain that where any sailor returns to shore and wants a glass of beer, or something stronger than beer, he will have a comfortable place to which to go, some place where he will not be a prey to strangers of one sort or another, and that he will get the very best that can be provided-not something that is drugged, bootlegged stuff or something that will do him injury. Liquor has its rightful place, and I presume that when the sailor comes in after having been frozen or half-frozen for weeks, passing through storms and terrible times, if he thinks a glass of liquor will do him good he should get it. I expect that he will have that privilege and that he will be given pure, unadulterated liquor under the best possible conditions. The department should see to it that he is not compelled to go to places where his health might be ruined, and unfit him to return to the ship.
The minister has quoted some verses and I was glad to hear him. He has the Scotch flair. What would you expect from a man named Angus Macdonald? It is a Scotch
War Appropriation-Naval Services

characteristic to love verses and I, too, have been thinking over some verses I have read. I do not believe the poet's name is known, and I am not quite sure whether the title of this particular poem is ""The Sea is His"", or ""The Sea is God's"". Two verses occur to me and I should like to quote them-I do so from memory:
Count me the splendid captains Who sailed with courage high
To chart the perillous waves unknown: Tell me where these men lie.
To light a path for ships to come They moored in Deadman's Quay.
The sea is God's, He made it,
But England shall keep it free.

As 1 repeat these lines I think of the admirals to whom the minister referred- Frobisher, Hawkins, Collingwood, Nelson, Jellicoe and Beatty, all those gallant men from away back, from the time of Drake, in the earliest days of the navy, when British sailors sailed the seas and founded those harbours and colonies that have made possible the commerce which has built up our empire. The other verse is this:
0 little land of England 0 mother of hearts too brave,
Men say the trust will pass from thee Who guardeth Nelson's grave.
Aye, but these braggarts shall learn Who'd hold the world in fee The Sea is God's, He made it,
But England shall keep it free.
Canada is doing a noble part to-day to help Britain in keeping the seas free.

1266488,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.15,1942-05-07,ead8ec08-81d6-44dd-b076-e1054fa170c7,ca.m.4581,Mr. REID:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,There are one or two questions which I wish to put to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, but before I do so I join with those who have given praise to the men who man our ships. Too much cannot be said of those who day after day toil in our Canadian ships. The minister this afternoon spoke about the numbers of men in the navy, and he gave a lengthy resume, one which we were all delighted to hear. Most. hon. members will be pleased to hear of the great number of ships and the numbers of men that comprise the Canadian navy. I say to the minister, keep up the good work, because the navy, of which the minister is head, is at present doing a splendid service. We have no doubt it will continue to do equally good work. The minister spoke of the training of seamen, personnel and so on. I will make this suggestion.

I have met many men in British Columbia who had been in the naval service either with Great Britain or in the Canadian navy during the last war, and these men have said to me: ""Why cannot our services be utilized? We were experienced seamen in those days and we did our duty. If the Canadian government

wants us, We are ready and willing to do the same again."" I think the country could very' well make use of the services of these men. They got their sea legs many years ago, and with very little training now they would once more render extremely valuable service.

Another suggestion. While we are waiting for ships, while we have a waiting list of four or five thousand men, it might be advisable to look into the idea of having some of these men placed on coastal ships.. 1266490,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.17,1942-05-07,99359485-a884-4818-b289-348ffbe33fb1,ca.m.7831,Mr. NOSE WORTHY:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I am sure every hon. member with the tang of the sea in his blood has been thrilled by the references made by the minister this afternoon to the great historical figures of British naval history. We have also been interested in the glowing picture he has given of a fast and greatly increasing Canadian navy. There are a few points on which he touched to which I should like to make reference and on which I think the committee might be entitled to further information.

The minister told us in round numbers of the increase which has taken place in the Canadian navy since the beginning of the war. He told us we now have a navy thirty times as great, I think he said, as at the beginning of the war. That in itself does not give us very much information, for my recollection of the Canadian navy at the beginning of the war is that it was very small indeed. He gave us the number of ships which have been added to the navy. I wonder if in order to round out that picture, he would be willing to give us a break-down of those figures showing the various classes of ships included in that total.

He spoke also of the duty and the great service rendered by the ships in convoying. We heard of 56,000,000 tons of goods convoyed safely across the ocean, and 9,000 ships. Would it be in the public interest for the minister to give us the other side of that picture? May we have from the minister the total value of ships and cargoes sailing from Canadian ports that have been lost during the war; first, those lost within convoys or while being convoyed, and second, those lost without convoy? No mention was made by the minister of the future programme pertaining to the building of merchant shipping; that I presume comes under another department. It is a matter very closely related to the navy, since our success in getting our goods delivered to the battle fronts depends to a large extent upon the number and nature of the merchant marine as well as upon the number of navy ships. I trust that at some later time in this debate we may be given a report of the programme for the building of merchant ships as well as ships for the navy.

At two or three points in his statement the minister referred to the matter of research, invention and so on. Could the minister tell us what organization exists to take advantage of Canadian engineering ingenuity and inventiveness for the inventing and production of new and improved types of ships, guns, et cetera, whether there is any organization of that kind or any council of marine and civil engineers employed in that particular field, or whether we take all our designs for ships and equipment and defence from the British navy?

A reference was made to the naval cadets. I have some knowledge of cadet training, some knowledge of the confusion which the training of three different classes of cadets is causing throughout the schools of the country at present. There is an undesirable competition and in some cases dissension and jealousy arising between the cadets of the different forces. There are one or two other matters to which I should like to refer briefly before six o'clock. The first is the establishment of the naval college on the Pacific coast. should be given to training them on the Atlantic coast and not removing them to the other coast. I do not mention this in any sectional way at all. Perhaps the minister, if he knows anything about it, will tell the committee and put the position right on paper so that the public may have the official view as to what was the trouble, where the responsibility is, and what is going to be done.
