I have before me a table of rates which, for men who are performing services such as those being performed by the men of the navy, are, in my opinion, a disgrace. I want to draw particular attention to them. It may be of some assistance to the minister in his representations to the treasury board. These are dependents' allowances, and the figures come from the minister's own department.

The marriage allowance for the wife is 75 cents a day, and 25 cents a day for each child. For other dependents, such as mother, dependent brother or sister or otherwise, it is 65 cents a day. The foregoing allowances are payable with the proviso that marriage allowance plus dependents' allowances shall not exceed a total of $2 per diem for officers, or SI .75 per diem for ratings. In effect, this means that a sailor who may be supporting a dependent mother, and is already in receipt, of SI .75 per diem by way of allowance, can receive only 25 cents per diem for the dependent mother. That, in my opinion, is something that should be rectified.

Dependents' allowance is graded according to the income of the dependent as follows-I want the minister to listen to these figures because I think there is something wrong with them. If the income per month is nil, the allowance per diem is 65 cents. If the income per month is $15, the allowance per diem is 50 cents. If the income per month is $10. the allowance per diem is 35 cents. According to the table the larger the income, the higher the allowance; there must be something wrong with those figures.

Further, it states that under a recent order in council the board may grant a supplementary award of dependents' allowance of 15 cents per diem to a dependent if, in its opinion, there are extenuating circumstances to warrant it; that at this point the functions
War Appropriation-Naval Services

of this board cease, but further assistance might be available to a dependent. In other words, as I understand it, this means that if, for example, the mother or the wife is not completely dependent and is receiving the maximum award under this supplementary assistance, in case of sickness and so forth the board has no authority to grant any additional allowance.

Then there is the dependents' board of trustees. It has a peculiar function. In cases of urgent need it may augment dependents' allowance ""by a special grant of an unspecified amount, provided that the dependents' allowance board has conceded dependency and that full award of dependent's allowance has been granted previously. Application for such grant should be directed to that board."" As I read that, the dependents' board of trustees has practically no function. It has no regulations to guide it; it is merely a matter of the board exercising its own opinion, without proper regulations to guide it and proper tables set out. In my opinion the board has only a very limited function; the whole thing is on a charity basis, and it is time that we showed our appreciation, at least to the extent of taking care of the dependents of the service we eulogized this afternoon.

I can readily understand the mind of a man who is on the water, and who knows the situation of his family. One case in particular has been brought to my attention, that of a radio operator who is on the water for eight, twelve or more months at a time. He has a wife and one child, and her total dependents' income is $29.50 a month. I do not consider that that woman is receiving an allowance; I say that she is on relief, because on that limited sum she cannot, in view of the present cost of living, maintain a home, including the cost of fuel and everything else in connection with it. The mind of that radio operator at sea must be in constant turmoil when he thinks of his family trying to eke out an existence on an allowance of that kind. I believe there is nothing that can break down the morale of a man any quicker than conditions of that kind. My experience has been that the man who serves in the army or navy is not concerned with himself. He offers himself in the service of his country, and, if necessary, his life is at stake. He is content to fight for his way of life. But meantime he is leaving his dependents in the care of the people at home charged with the responsibility of running the country. The least he can expect is that during the time he is separated from his country, and the time he is prepared to lay down his life, if neces-
sary, the family he has left behind should be at least maintained with some degree of comfort.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

allowance is somewhat lower, being only $7.50 a month per child. A man in the navy who lives out of barracks receives a somewhat higher allowance than a man in the army similarly situated. When I stated on November 11 last that we expected shortly to undertake the building of destroyers I spoke correctly. But my hon. friend will remember that on December 7 the United States became involved in war, and the steel for destroyers, or at any rate certain kinds of steel which is not manufactured in this country-steel which we had hoped first, to get from Great Britain and then turned to the United States to secure- that steel was denied us. On the outbreak of war, the United States government and manufacturers naturally decided that they should keep all their steel there until the situation became clearer. We have received certain shipments of steel from the United States; arrangements have been made for the construction of destroyers at Halifax; things are being shaped up, and the keel steel will arrive, I believe, very soon. Make no mistake; every effort is being made to get it. But my hon. friend will understand how difficult it is for a country that finds itself plunged into war, and has a tremendous shipbuilding programme of its own-an inconceivably big programme in the matter of both merchant ships and war ships-to let steel go even to a friendly country such as ours. But I think that difficulty is being pretty well overcome now. We shall have the steel, and the keels of those destroyers will be laid in a very short time.

1266574,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.101,1942-05-07,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. DIEFENBAKER:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,There is one

phase of the work in which the navy is engaged that was not dealt with at any length by the minister in the admirable address he gave this afternoon. Were it not for the fact that from time to time reports are given in the British House of Commons in connection therewith, I would not bring it up. The contribution of the Canadian navy and all it means, the great sacrifices being made by the men of that service and of the merchant marine, after the recital that has been given us to-day will make us all realize even more clearly that the success of the united nations depends upon keeping the sea lanes open. During the past couple of weeks various statements have been made in the United States senate and house of representatives in regard to the problem of keeping the sea lanes open, and in particular to the submarine campaign going on on the Atlantic, designed to prevent shipments of tanks and munitions and aeroplanes to Russia, to the near east and to Great Britain. According to information published in Washington on April 17 last, considerable improvement is taking place as far as submarine attacks on the Atlantic are concerned, and in the issue of the United States News which I have before me it is stated that the great problem facing the united nations to-day is to keep the sea lanes open, and that for every two ships now being launched by the united nations, three ships are being sunk by axis submarines. It adds that there has been improvement recently.

I do not want to ask any questions that might in any way tend to endanger the safety of the united nations or Canada. But the other day the senior ranking officer of the navy made a speech in which he pointed out the serious situation on the Atlantic. If that statement be true, the people of Canada should know and realize the condition and the position in which we are. The people of Canada to-day want to know the facts, but only those the revelation of which could be of no assistance to the enemy. Is the minister in a position to-night to tell us whether or not there is an improvement on the Atlantic, whether or not we are winning on the one front where it is necessary to win in order to secure victory on land? I should like him to tell us if he can what expansion, if any, is anticipated in the navy during the coming year. We have heard frequently that the government of Canada has a plan for Canada's part in the war effort. Is that plan the exten-
War Appropriation-Naval Services
sion of the army, further expansion in the air force, the extension of the navy or an acceleration of munitions production?

We heard to-day an address eloquent in its terms, inspiring in its viewpoint, telling Canadians what Canadian navy men are doing and the wonderful advances made by our navy. I think all of us are proud of the work that has been done in the expansion of the Canadian navy, proud of the contributions it is making, proud of the acceleration in the service it renders, as the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) said with the pride that must be felt by a father whose son is in that navy. We are proud of our navy, and we do not want any information that might in any way aid the enemy. But if the situation is bad on the Atlantic, let the people of Canada know it; let them realize what we are up against; for if there is one thing that the people of Canada must have to-day, it is a message challenging them to greater effort, a message from those in authority, a message that has not yet been given. We should know that the challenge we face is of our survival. What are the dangers that we must overcome? What are the sacrifices the people must make individually in order to secure victory? To-day the minister went a long way in giving detailed information. I have refrained from asking some of the questions which the minister has felt free to answer; but without going into any elucidation which could be construed in any way as being of assistance to those who to-day are our enemies, I ask him to let the people know what the situation is and what our responsibilities are, so that we may realize what we are up against and what further responsibilities we must undertake. The men in the factory, the men who produce destroyers and other ships of war, will have a renewed determination if they know the challenge that is before them.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266575,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.102,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,My hon. friend has raised a point, I must say, with great fairness and courtesy, and with due regard for the importance of the subject. I could give him an answer now, but I should prefer to wait until to-morrow in order that I may do justice to my hon. friend, to the manner in which he has raised the question, and to the importance of the question itself.

I know the statement to which my hon. friend refers. It was made by the chief of the naval staff a few weeks ago, as to the presence of submarines on our coasts. He expressed the view that this year, submarines might well be found operating in the gulf of St. Lawrence and perhaps in the St. Lawrence river itself. There is no doubt that this is a very distinct possibility. There is no reason why sub-

marines could not get into the gulf of St. Lawrence and operate there. There is every likelihood that they may do so. As I said this afternoon, already they have come within sight of our eastern shores; they have come within sight of the shores of the United States, both east and west, and there is no reason why they may not continue that practice.

As to the general situation on the Atlantic, as I have said I should prefer to give a little thought to such a statement. The Atlantic is a large body of water. The line between eastern Canada and Great Britain is one thing; the coastal lines up and down, north and south, are another. It would be true to say that it is the north and south line, the coastal traffic line, which in the last three months has sustained the most severe attack. More than that I should not care to say at this moment. But to-morrow afternoon, if my hon. friend will grant me that much grace, after a little more preparation, I should like to make a statement.

1266578,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.105,1942-05-07,b7be8f86-27c2-4da9-a780-2d2bb5edfa31,ca.m.646,Mr. HANSELL:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I anticipate that if the minister brings down a statement which shows that there will continue to be a difference in those allowances, a few questions will be asked, and a discussion of the subject will be precipitated. I can understand that there may be a difference between the pay of a plasterer and the pay of a carpenter, though they are both engaged in the building and construction industry. does the wife of a soldier; surely she wears just as many clothes, so I see no reason for that difference. If, after this statement to-morrow, a difference still exists, I think the minister will have to be prepared to answer this question: What is -the determining factor which causes the dependents' allowance in one service to be different from that in another? 1266579,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.106,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I should like to answer some questions, in the order in which they were asked this afternoon. First there were questions asked by the hon. member for Yale, as to training, the standard *of training in the Canadian navy, and whether we are taking in boy seamen, cadets and midshipmen. The answer to these three questions is that at the moment we are not taking in boy seamen or cadets or midshipmen. There is a small number of these men in the Canadian navy, from previous years, but no more are being allowed to enlist for the time being. The hon. member also asked whether naval cadets still went to England for training, as they did in peace time. The answer is no. We believe that our own naval college at Esquimalt will take care of that.

Then my hon. friend asked for a brief description of the training establishments at each coast. I can deal with that matter only in a very general way, but I may tell him that there are barracks at both Halifax and Esquimalt where men are lodged and fed. Unfortunately there is not enough barracks accommodation to take care of all the men, so in the Canadian navy we have some seven thousand men who have to live and eat out of quarters. But we have barracks at these places. We have various training buildings, gunnery schools, torpedo schools, schools wherein submarine detection instruments are studied. We have a signal school now situated at St. Hyacinthe, Quebec. We have one radio direction finding school, where instruction is given in that very important work-and so on-at each coast.
Then, I am asked if the men receive refresher courses before going to ships, such
as corvettes. The answer would be, not in all cases. Some men would go right out of their training course, and sign on a corvette.

A good engineer might go right in. Others might take preliminary training. A very young man might be sent to one of these five or six training schools. But the chief refresher course for any rank would be for the man who had been at sea for a time and who is considered to have special aptitude for gunnery, torpedo work, signalling or anti-submarine work. He would be taken ashore, and perhaps given special training in that type of work.

Then the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Blackmore) raised a question as to why we do not endeavour to build up here a navy which would be auxiliary to the Royal Navy. He went on to say that we should be strong and that we must build for the future. I must say I agree very largely with what the hon. member has said. That brings up the point discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), as to disarmament. That subject might hardly come within the scope of this debate, but offhand I would say that disarmament is a splendid thing-if everybody disarms. But it is a ridiculous thing if only a few disarm, and others are allowed to go on arming-as they did in the last ten years. They did go on arming at a furious rate, while countries against whom they were arming did very little but talk about it. World disarmament practised by everybody is excellent. Disarmament practised by a few amounts to something very like suicide for those who disarm.

Recreational facilities at Halifax was another subject mentioned by the hon. member. Some question was raised by the leader of the opposition with respect to the Ajax club. However, some difficulty arose in connection with the securing of a liquor permit. I had nothing to do with that. It was located very close to a church, unfortunately, and some objection was taken from that quarter.

I may say, however-and I wish my hon. friend who is honorary president for Ontario of the navy league were here-that the Navy League of Canada has undertaken to do something which I believe will be much better than any club facilities of the ordinary kind could be. They have agreed to take over those splendid athletic grounds in Halifax known as the Wanderers' club grounds. Hon. members representing Halifax will know the location. It is a very beautiful site, with trees growing all around, the whole being surrounded by a high board fence. It has been used for many years as an athletic field for the playing of football, baseball and cricket, and it possesses an excellent running track. It is the intention of the Navy League of Canada to have at that point facilities for sailors, not only to provide them with ordinary canteen facilities for the purchase of cigarettes, and so on, but to provide athletic equipment whereby men coming in from boats may play football, baseball, cricket or bowls, or any of those other sports which

naval personnel is proceeding in close collaboration with the British navy? Most of us in Canada have the conviction that the British navy is second to none with respect to its traditions and its achievements all through the years. I believe that the British navy contains officers and men the like of whom the world has never seen in point of real effectiveness on the water. I have no doubt that in Britain the schemes and plans of training of men for the navy are in a highly perfected condition, and I have been wondering whether the Department of National Defence for Naval Services is collaborating with the British naval authorities so that some part of their tremendously important experience is made available to Canadian naval officers and men. I would couple with that an inquiiy as to how closely the work of the Canadian navy is joined with that of the British navy in the general war operations at this time. We in Canada are amateurs in naval affairs compared with the seamen of the motherland, and it would seem to me wholly within the realm of common sense that we should seek, wherever possible, to take advantage of the work which has been and is being done by the British government in the development of sea power efficiency, an achievement which, as I have said before, approximates the best that the world has known.

All senior officers of the rank of captain and above have had experience on British ships, and even some below the rank of captain have done their year or two on British ships of various types-battleships, cruisers and the like. ,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Angus MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266613,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.140,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,The common type of vessel used in convoying before the war would be the destroyer, but since the beginning of this war we have developed the corvette, which is cheaper and much easier to build than the destroyer. It has not the speed or the power, but it is a very useful vessel to attack submarines. Even the mine-sweeper, which is very much the same as the corvette in some respects, can be used as an escort ship. Any ship that can carry depth charges and move a little faster than the submarine under water is of some use as an escort for convoys, but I should name the typical escort for convoys as destroyers and corvettes. The great battleship, I suppose, would not be used normally for the escort of convoys unless it was a convoy of exceptional importance, a very large troop convoy, where you wanted a battleship to deal with some other battleship. But if you are not going to deal with battleships but want to hunt submarines, the destroyer and the corvette will do the trick better than the battleship.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266614,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.141,1942-05-07,795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1,ca.m.1278,Mr. GRAYDON:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Is there any scheme of coordination between the work of the air force here and that of the navy, as there has been in so many other countries since the
War Appropriation-Naval Services

war began? If one judges the news correctly, the question of air protection in the naval force has reached the position where air protection is practically the most essential part of some of the work the navy has to do. Could the minister tell us what scheme has been adopted between our air force and our navy with respect to any events that may occur in the future which would necessitate close collaboration between the two branches?

,National Government,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266615,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.142,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,That is a very interesting question, in answer to which perhaps full details cannot be given in the very nature of things, but I may say this to my hon. friend. Take the east coast where there is a naval establishment and also an air force. There is a very close degree of cooperation. Air patrols go out so many hundred miles over the water daily. Many patrols go out; they report to the naval authorities and naval vessels anything which they see, and that experience in itself is very valuable as a lesson in cooperation. What my hon. friend raises primarily, I think, is the point that has come to the fore so much in recent months, and that is that naval power alone, if attacked by air power, is at a great disadvantage. That, unfortunately for us, has proved only too true in recent months. Torpedo bombers diving down and launching torpedoes which go over the water have proved singularly effective against some of our ships. We have not had that form of attack on our coast. We have not had surface attacks on our coasts, but when it comes I believe the experience which the air force has already gained, and the navy as well, by cooperating with and reporting one to the other, signalling one to the other, and collecting information for their mutual advantage, will be quite valuable.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266616,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.143,1942-05-07,d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38,ca.m.4292,Mr. DOUGLAS (Weyburn):,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Have any
steps been taken to develop any type of fleet air arm?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Thomas Clement (Tommy) Douglas,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266617,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.144,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,No, not yet. We have not got that yet.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266618,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.145,1942-05-07,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury):,Leader of the Official Opposition,NAVAL SERVICES,,,That

situation obtains in the United States. Would the minister care to express an opinion-perhaps he would be too modest-as to the advantage of the navy having its own air force, as they have in the United States, compared with following the practice we have of a separate force working in cooperation with the navy? There are two schools of thought about that in the United States, as I have read-and elsewhere too, a colleague of mine suggests. In England I have heard a good deal of murmur, shall I say, on the part of the senior service in the navy that

they do not have control of the air force on this patrol work. It is a matter of opinion, I suppose, and I am wondering what the minister's opinion is, if he has formed one. There are two distinct schools of thought about it in the United States and possibly in England. Has Canada developed any thought along that line?

,National Government,,Richard Burpee Hanson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266619,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.146,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I do not know that I have any definite view on that point; I have no aeroplanes in any event. But the British system is, of course, to have an air force, an army and a navy. The navy has some little air force of its own. It has a fleet air arm, and in addition to that there is cooperation between the navy and the regular air force. The United States system does not provide for any separate air force. The army has its own air arm, and so has the navy. There are two views about it. One view is that this new thing, this air force, a new up-and-coming element, should not be checked and held down by the older service, that they should not shackle the new to the old. That view has prevailed in the United States up to the moment, though I cannot say what changes time may bring. I have no definite views on the matter myself. Sometimes one works well, sometimes the other.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266620,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.147,1942-05-07,043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6,ca.m.6101,Mr. NICHOLSON:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Has any thought been given by the minister's department to the question of providing housing for the families of men of the navy? In the United States large appropriations have been set aside for providing suitable houses in locations where large numbers of naval men and officers are stationed. The figures which the minister has placed on the record to-night give some indication of the very serious problem existing in many parts of Canada. For example, he informs us that 10,135 have joined the navy from Ontario, 2,241 from Manitoba, 1,890 from Saskatchewan, 2,425 from Alberta. It naturally follows that men from these inland provinces are going to find themselves at sea eventually, and owing to the very small allowances available hitherto there is not much chance of these men seeing their families very often. I know a critical situation has already developed. Large numbers of people have flocked to Halifax. The Department of Munitions and Supply has assumed responsibility for building temporary houses for people in cities and towns where war industries have been established. In Halifax houses have been built to accommodate people who have gone there for employment in connection with munitions and supply work, but the families of men of the navy are not permitted to occupy these temporary war-time houses. The
War Appropriation-Naval Services

Minister of National Defence was asked the other night whether his branch had given consideration to the providing of houses near military establishments, and he stated that so far no such plans had been undertaken. It would seem to me that at this stage, with a navy thirty times larger than Canada had at the commencement of the war, and the very large sums that have been appropriated for naval services, some consideration should be given to what appears to be an essential part of naval activities, that is providing some place for the families of the men and their officers to live.

The figures that the hon. member for Cape Breton South placed before us this evening showed that a wife with three children would be allowed $45 a month. Assuming that she had $20 a month assigned pay, that would provide $65 a month. It is usually taken for granted that not more than 25 per cent of the monthly income should be spent on house rent. Twenty-five per cent of $65 equals $16 and some cents available for house rent. My information is that in Halifax it is impossible to secure any sort of suitable quarters for that amount. It seems to me that since the government so far has not seen fit to permit Wartime Housing Limited to make their houses available for the families of those in the army, the navy and the air force, either these departments must undertake this very essential service, or the necessary changes must be made to permit Wartime Housing Limited to provide a sufficient number of houses in centres to which large migrations have taken place. Is the minister prepared to make a statement as to the consideration that has been given to this question and whether some policy might be outlined?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Alexander Malcolm Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266621,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.148,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Yes; a great deal of consideration has been given to that problem. For some time the naval authorities at Halifax have been investigating the number of families that are there and in need of housing, or better housing than they have been able to secure up to the moment.

The problem is not very simple; like many of these problems it becomes more and more complex as you get into it. As far as the navy is concerned there are only two points that would trouble it-Halifax and perhaps Esquimalt. Our great concentrations of men are at these points. But the army has, say fifty places in Canada where camps have been set up; the air force has a good many; and at once the question is raised, ""Are we to build houses at every place where we have a camp, in order to permit soldiers' families to come fMr. Nicholson.]

there and visit their men?"" I think something has to be done for the families of ratings, but I think that must be coupled with this provision, that a soldier who goes to Halifax to get on a ship and perhaps has to wait there a week or two, cannot expect the government to guarantee that he is going to get accommodation for his family at that point. What the Department of Munitions and Supply has done in the case of industrial plants is to say, ""These workmen are going to be here continuously up to the end of the war; they have to have their families with them."" We may have to say the same thing in the case of workmen in the naval dockyards who are permanently employed there and want to bring their families there. I can see no distinction between the two cases. But I can see a good deal of distinction between that and the case of a sailor who comes to Halifax for a week or two, or perhaps a month, out of the year and wants to have his family there. I think we shall have to say to these people, ""No, it is all right for you to come to Halifax, but you cannot expect us to provide a house for your family."" In -the case of men permanently stationed there, I regard the situation as completely different, and I agree with what my hon. friend said in -that respect.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266622,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.149,1942-05-07,29020af7-698a-475d-8d4d-dd9f2528d390,ca.m.3136,Mr. HAZEN:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,The hon. member for Lake Centre this evening brought up the matter of the loss of shipping. That is a very important matter. The minister has told us that he will make a statement about it to-morrow. I had intended to refer to it briefly and to ask one or two questions. If the minister will permit me, I will put them on the record. I do not expect him to answer them now. Perhaps he will not consider it advisable to answer them at all, but if he thinks it is not against the public interest to answer -them, I hope he will do so when he makes his statement.

The questions have to do with the convoying of ships. If ships travelling along the sea lanes of the Atlantic coast are not convoyed, is the failure to provide convoys for these ships due (1) to lack of cooperation between one defence department and another either here or in the United States? (2) to any lack of cooperation between Canada and the United States? (3) -to a shortage of ships in the navy?

,National Government,,Douglas King Hazen,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=29020af7-698a-475d-8d4d-dd9f2528d390&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266623,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.150,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I think my hon. friend can make a pretty shrewd guess as to which is the correct answer. I should certainly say, as I said before, that when we speak of the Atlantic we must remember that the route from eastern Canada to the United Kingdom is one thing, the north-
War Appropriation-Naval Services
south route is another. There is certainly no lack of cooperation between any departments in this country in that regard.

I can answer question No. 1 immediately. As to question No. 2: ""Is it due to any lack of cooperation between Canada and the United States?"" I should say there is no lack of cooperation between these two countries in that regard. Then as to question No. 3: ""Is it due to lack of ships?"" I can only say to my hon. friend that he is getting warmer and warmer as he goes along with his questions.

Mr. MacIiNNIS: A short time ago the minister mentioned naval dock yards and said it might become necessary to provide homes for the workers in those yards. How many dock yards are being operated by the navy department at present, and how many workers are engaged in those yards?

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266624,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.151,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,It would take me some little time to get the number of men. The main docks, of course, in which the navy is interested, are the dock at Esquimalt; the floating dock at Prince Rupert-of course these docks do not belong to us, but we use them-and the naval dockyard at Halifax. There is also a dock yard at Esquimalt which is ours, in addition to the drydock. Then we are constructing small docks at various points along the eastern coast. They are really marine railways, which can take ships up to 3,000 tons. Perhaps five or six of these are being constructed now. They are really small docks in themselves, for the accommodation of ships from destroyers down, and I think they will prove very useful.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266625,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.152,1942-05-07,b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442,ca.m.5903,Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury):,Leader of the Official Opposition,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Those are principally for cleaning and repairs?

,National Government,,Richard Burpee Hanson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266626,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.153,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,Yes, repairs and refits.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266627,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.154,1942-05-07,44449e3c-562a-4461-aa3d-ae59eb3971cd,ca.m.7929,Mr. NOSEWORTIIY:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,The minister told us there was no organization within his department for carrying on research into design and construction, or improvements in ships of the navy. Would he tell us by whom and where the ships now being constructed were designed?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Joseph William Noseworthy,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=44449e3c-562a-4461-aa3d-ae59eb3971cd&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266628,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.155,1942-05-07,4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1,ca.m.6010,Mr. STIRLING:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,That is very closely akin to a matter about which I was going to ask the minister, if the hon. member will permit me to interrupt. As I understand it, in a general way we have accepted the design and blueprints of the vessels which are being built for us, that is for the navy, by the

Department of Munitions and Supply, from the Royal Navy, and those designs are based on the experience they have obtained over the years. When this matter is under discussion with men in the industry, this point has come up again and again. Are we adapting these designs, these working drawings and the materials which are used in the construction, to the facilities that we have at our hand? The question came up with regard to a contract for some boats; I forget the description of them now. The specifications called for copper air tanks, and it was pointed out to me that for the purposes for which these boats are going to be used by the navy, galvanized iron tanks would be just as good, last pretty well as long as the boat itself might be expected to last, and be considerably cheaper, and that the material would be more easily obtained. The same argument applied to the rather expensive use of teak in finishing. Are there not Canadian woods just as good for the purpose? In the case of rowlocks, as another example, on a pinnace, a whaler, or a pulling boat in the Royal Navy, they have had machined rowlocks since away back, but in recent years I believe that in this country we have substituted stamped rowlocks.

These matters would affect not only the economy of the work to be done but also certainly the time which would be occupied therein. This was emphasized in my mind at the time General MeNaughton was oyer here bringing his knowledge of Canadian manufacturing to bear on the contracts which were being carried out in this country. The minister will remember that it was with some pleasure that General MeNaughton was able to point out that Great Britain is now becoming more and more interested in changes in design which Canadian engineers and Canadian industry are ready to make so as to adapt the pieces of machinery being made to the method of construction in force on this continent. If that is the case with regard to munitions, using the word in its larger sense, it appears to me that it could well be adapted to the construction of the craft whose design we have taken, I believe in almost every instance, from Great Britain.

,National Government,,Grote Stirling,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266629,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.156,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I may say to the hon. gentleman who asked the question originally that we have not had in this country a constructor branch in the navy; that is, we have not had a branch in which men would be engaged in planning and revising the construction of ships. We are now just beginning the organization of such a branch, under Captain Harrison, and I have
War Appropriation-Naval Services
every hope that this branch will expand and become a very useful part of the naval service.

The hon. member for Yale is quite right; up to the present we have had to rely upon the British admiralty for designs; and with the exception of the naval dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt, where the navy itself might undertake to build whatever small boats it needed, we have followed the British design. Wherever Canadian woods can be substituted for woods that would require to be imported, that is done; but there are cases where that is very difficult. My hon. friend mentioned teak. We have not yet discovered, I am given to understand, a proper substitute for teak, meaning by that a substitute which will embody all the qualities which teak is supposed to possess and which will in every way serve the purpose. I believe that experiments are being carried out all the time. Woods are being tested for this and that, to discover whether they will be suitable as substitutes for mahogany, teak, oak or other kinds of wood that are specified in the British -designs. I think that is all I can say in reply to my hon. friend.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266630,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.157,1942-05-07,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. MacINNIS:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,What is the policy of the minister's department in regard to the transportation of officers and ratings, as between the two railway systems. There are great numbers of naval men travelling at the present time, and I was wondering about the policy of the department with regard to the road over which the men should travel.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Angus MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266631,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.158,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,The regulations I have here state that the railroads are to be used according to the best interests of the naval service. There is always some wrangling between the roads. In the last few days I have had telegrams from one of the railroad brotherhoods saying that there is a hearing taking place before the railway committee, and all that sort of thing. About a year ago the naval service called in representatives of the two roads and said, ""Try to agree on some division among yourselves. Agree on a division of territory, or some other division; and let us have your decision."" They did agree. Later, some of the senior people of one of the roads said they knew nothing about this agreement. Later still, however, they said, ""I guess there was an agreement, and we will accept it.""

The agreement w-orked out so that within a certain territory naval personnel would travel by the Canadian National Railways, and within certain other territory they would travel by the Canadian Pacific Railway. As a matter of fact, the agreement works out so that one railway gets considerably more than the other.
LMr. Macdonald (Kingston City).]

However, I cannot go into all the details of the arrangement. One railway says, ""We get a little more money, but we have to hand over a good deal of it to the other road. While we sell the tickets, a good deal of travelling is done on the other road."" All I can say to my hon. friend is that we have had these two representatives meet with naval officers. They worked out an agreement and signed it and, for the moment, I think we had better let it stand at that.

,Liberal,,Angus Lewis Macdonald,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266632,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.159,1942-05-07,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. MacINNIS:,,NAVAL SERVICES,,,What is the number of naval passengers transported by each road in the last two years, or since the beginning of the war?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Angus MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1266633,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.160,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,I cannot give that information at the moment. It would be rather difficult to get, unless a certain year were indicated, say the year 1941. I could give my hon. friend totals, if it would serve any purpose. Last year, in freight, passenger and express receipts the Canadian National Railways got something like

column2: from us, and the Canadian Pacific Railway got something less than 8600,000.- As I have said, the Canadian National will argue that their business was not profitable, and that they had to give away a lot of this money to the Canadian Pacific. However, they will have to fight that out among themselves. They have agreed to it, and we will let it stand.

1266643,ca.proc.d.1942-05-07.6.170,1942-05-07,2b74f178-e704-4a9d-8811-9cd1eaf94f62,ca.m.4308,Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City):,Minister of National Defence for Naval Services,NAVAL SERVICES,,,There is a very considerable waiting list for officers and men. There are probably 4,000 or 5,000 men whose applications are on file but who have not yet been taken into the navy. The list remains constantly about that figure. Some of those who applied a year ago or six months ago may be in by now. Their places on the waiting list are taken by more recent applicants. Therefore there is that waiting list of

column2: or 5,000 men waiting to get into the navy.

column1: The same is true with respect to officers. Selection boards which go around the country inform me that if they want thirty officers, usually about 100 apply. It is useless to take more than are needed. The result is that the other seventy have to wait, and take their chances when the next, board comes round in a few months. Of course, the seventy may go in as ratings. It is absolutely impossible to take into the navy all who apply.

Mark you, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Royal has said that a year ago men were encouraged to go into the navy. However, as far as I know, the navy has never spent five cents on recruiting. I have seen posters showing a picture of an army soldier, an airman and a naval rating; but so far as I know, we have never spent anything on recruiting literature, posters, advertisements or anything of that kind. Still, the number of men is there. We just cannot handle them; that is all.

Nova Scotia has given us about 3,900 naval recruits. That is a very large proportion, larger, I believe, than that of any other province with the exception of Prince Edward Island, where the proportion is slightly higher. That is a much higher proportion than has been given by any other place. A good many of these men have been bred to the sea and have found their way into the navy. Saskatchewan has a greater population than Nova Scotia, and we have had some 1,890 men from there, something less than half the Nova Scotia figure. That is no reflection upon Saskatchewan because it has probably given more men to the army. But it would be a great mistake to confine naval recruiting to the eastern and western shores of this country. Recruits from the prairies make excellent seamen. Their physique is good, and there are really many things to be done on a ship besides sailing it. There is gunnery, torpedo work, signalling work, anti-submarine detection, radio work and mechanical work of all kinds. There is a place on a ship for a man who is accustomed to mechanical work. The navy tries to get men from every province of Canada, but inevitably it will draw more men from the provinces by the sea.

interesting question with reference to cooperation between the navy and the air force on the coasts. Could the minister carry his answer a step further and give us some information with reference to the coordination of services on the coasts. Of necessity the navy is primarily concerned with seeing that convoys get safely across the ocean, but there is another task within their jurisdiction, the defence of Canadian shores. In the last few months another stage in the war has developed. There is now the possibility of fairly large surface ships approaching Canada, not so much with the idea of invasion as with the idea of shelling naval installations or even landing marine parties to destroy radio equipment, dock yards and so on. A military commander has been appointed for each of the coasts, and last week the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) explained something of the cooperation that exists between the military command and the air force.

Would the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services explain how the navy fits into this picture? Will the naval patrol vessels-I suppose torpedo boats would be mainly used against surface craft-come directly under command of the military commander responsible for the defence of the coast, or is there merely some cooperation? The minister said before that there was always cooperation. Naturally we would expect that, but more and more the lesson that this war seems to be teaching the united nations is that in many instances coordination is not enough, that in modern warfare the different arms of the service must be synchronized with the command under one individual when there is a specific task in mind. Could the minister tell us how the naval forces on the coasts tie in with the military command?
